passage:
Sabina: Hey. I saw the thread. You don't have to explain anything.
Tanvir: I can't stop reading it. Two thousand comments about my talk.
Sabina: Okay. Can we do one thing? Mute the thread and turn notifications off for tonight. I'll stay on this chat.
Tanvir: What if it gets worse
Sabina: Then we deal with it together. I've saved the ones that are plain abuse and I'll report them from my side too. You don't have to look at them.
Tanvir: Rohan posted a joke about it. Meher liked it. Kunal hasn't said anything at all.
Sabina: That's on them. I'm bringing dinner at 8. Just food, no talking about it unless you want to.
Tanvir: ok. thank you
Sabina: I'm here till you fall asleep.

qa.q: At what time is Sabina bringing dinner?
qa.a: Sabina is bringing dinner at 8.

qa.q: Why might Tanvir keep reading the thread even though it hurts?
qa.a: Tanvir feels exposed and may fear missing the next comment, so reading feels unavoidable even though it deepens the hurt.

qa.q: What did Sabina suggest first to help Tanvir?
qa.a: Sabina suggested muting the thread and turning notifications off for the night while staying on the chat.

qa.q: What might Sabina be feeling while promising to stay on the chat till Tanvir falls asleep?
qa.a: Sabina is probably worried about Tanvir and protective, which is why Sabina saves and reports the abusive comments and plans to bring dinner at 8.

grounding: Someone messages the target of a pile-on privately, helps them stop reading comments and reports the abuse, offering steady human contact.

passage:
By evening every phone in town had the clip of Anirban stumbling over the welcome speech at the school function. Jatin found him on the roof of the tuition centre, phone in his hand, thumb still scrolling. “Give it here for a bit,” Jatin said quietly, and Anirban did. Jatin switched off the comments, then sat on the parapet beside him with two cups of tea from the stall below.

Down there a few boys were still laughing at the clip. Pintu looked away as Jatin passed.

“Let's not read it tonight,” Jatin said. Later he helped Anirban report the cruellest messages and block the accounts. When Anirban's mother called up the stairs for dinner, Jatin went down with him. “I'll walk you to school tomorrow.” Anirban nodded, eyes on his tea.

qa.q: Where did Jatin find Anirban?
qa.a: Jatin found Anirban on the roof of the tuition centre.

qa.q: What does Anirban's nod with eyes on the tea suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Anirban is tired and hurt but grateful, quietly accepting company because words are hard.

qa.q: What steps did Jatin take to help besides staying nearby?
qa.a: Jatin switched off the comments, helped Anirban report the cruellest messages and block the accounts.

qa.q: What might Pintu feel while looking away as Jatin passes?
qa.a: Pintu might feel a flicker of guilt or embarrassment about laughing at the clip, and also worry about being the next target.

grounding: A person helps the target of an online pile-on stop reading comments, reports abuse and stays close, valuing steady contact over public defence.

subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
passage:
Ivan's short video review of a Prague restaurant had gone viral for the wrong reason: he'd mispronounced the chef's name, and people decided he was mocking her. By Sunday there were thousands of comments, some threatening.
His friend Hana didn't post a defence. She messaged him privately: “Hey. Are you reading them?”
“All of them,” Ivan wrote back.
“Stop. Give me your login for an hour. I'll turn off comments and report the threats. Go for a walk. I'll call you at six.”
He hesitated, then sent it.
Hana reported eleven threatening accounts. At six she called. Ivan sounded tired but steadier. “I thought everyone hated me.” “Not everyone,” Hana said. “Not me.”

qa.q: How many threatening accounts did Hana report?
qa.a: Hana reported eleven threatening accounts.

qa.q: How was Ivan feeling when he said everyone hated him?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and ashamed, as if everyone was against him after reading all the comments.

qa.q: Why was Hana's private help more useful than a public defence?
qa.a: She stopped him reading, reported the threats and stayed in touch by phone, which gave him real support without adding to the noise.

qa.q: How might the chef have felt about the viral video?
qa.a: She might have felt mixed, perhaps hurt at first by the mispronunciation, and uneasy about the anger done in her name.

grounding: Shows a friend privately messaging a pile-on target, helping her friend stop reading comments and reporting abuse.

subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
passage:
In the hospital's admin office, Lalit had gone pale. A post he'd written about long waiting times had been shared by a news page, and hundreds of people were calling him a liar and a traitor to the hospital. Some knew his full name and ward.
Neelam, from the next desk, saw his face. She didn't comment online. She took him to the pantry and made him tea.
“Mute the app,” she said gently. “Just for today. I'll sit with you.”
He muted it. His hands were shaking.
“Now, the ones that mention your address, let's screenshot them.” She helped him collect six, then walked with him to the IT and HR office before lunch. The HR officer took the complaint and asked security to watch his ward that week.

qa.q: How many threatening messages did they collect?
qa.a: They collected six.

qa.q: How was Lalit feeling when his hands were shaking?
qa.a: He was frightened and overwhelmed by hundreds of people calling him a liar, some knowing his name and ward.

qa.q: What did Neelam do well, and why did it help?
qa.a: She gave him steady company, helped him mute the app, collected the threats and went with him to HR the same day, which kept him safe.

qa.q: How might the HR officer see Neelam's role?
qa.a: The HR officer probably sees her as a calm, useful colleague who helped Lalit report it properly and quickly.

grounding: Shows a colleague supporting a pile-on target privately, helping him stop reading and reporting threats, rather than defending him publicly.

passage:
Hi Suraj,
I'm not going to comment on the post. I think you've had enough comments for one lifetime.
I just wanted you to know I'm here. That video from the wedding, the one where you tripped into the cake, it's not the end of anything. In two weeks the internet will be laughing at someone else.
Please stop reading the comments. Seriously. Delete the app for a few days if you can. If anyone sends you anything threatening, forward it to me and I'll help you report it.
I'll come over on Saturday with samosas, and we can watch the match and talk about anything except cake.
Call me anytime, even at 2 am.
Naveen

qa.q: What did Suraj trip into in the video?
qa.a: Suraj tripped into the cake.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling while writing this?
qa.a: Naveen felt concerned and protective, wanting Suraj to feel less alone during the pile-on.

qa.q: What does Naveen offer that helps most?
qa.a: Steady private contact: advice to stop reading, help with reporting threats, and a Saturday visit, instead of a public defence.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel after reading the message?
qa.a: Suraj would likely feel comforted and less alone, knowing a friend is there even at 2 am.

grounding: A friend writes privately to a pile-on target, urging the friend to stop reading comments, offering to report abuse and to visit.

subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
passage:
I'm Tanvir, and I run a small baking page, so I've seen how fast the internet turns.
Last year my friend Zeenat posted a review of a café that she thought was fair. By morning, three thousand strangers were calling her a liar and worse; the café's fans had found her. Our friends' group was full of "Did you see?" and long public comments defending her, which only brought more people to the post.
I didn't comment. I messaged her: "I'm here. Don't read it. Want me to come over?" I went, with samosas. We sat on her floor, and I turned off her notifications. I reported the three accounts that posted her address and helped her block them. Mostly, we watched old cartoons.
She told me later that the public defences made her feel like a spectacle. The friend on her floor made her feel like a person.

qa.q: How many strangers were calling Zeenat a liar by morning?
qa.a: Three thousand strangers.

qa.q: How did the public defences make Zeenat feel?
qa.a: Zeenat felt exposed, "like a spectacle", even though her friends meant well.

qa.q: Which of Tanvir's steps mattered most?
qa.a: Messaging privately, being physically there, turning off notifications and reporting the accounts that shared her address.

qa.q: What would have changed if Tanvir had only posted a public defence?
qa.a: Zeenat would still be alone with her phone, and the post might have drawn even more strangers into the pile-on.

grounding: Shows a friend supporting a pile-on target with private messages, company, a break from the comments and reporting abuse, rather than public defence.
